## Status: draft, unreviewed
Built from a Route53 hosted-zone export for `bioconductor.org` (166 records, reviewed
2026-09) plus a direct HTTPS probe of every resolvable hostname in it — not just the
DNS target, but what each one actually serves today. Satisfies the M1 tasks "decide
`www.`/`secure.` and satellite hostnames" and "cutover runbook page (DNS,
verification, rollback)" from the [roadmap](roadmap.qmd). Not yet walked with the core
team — treat every status and finding below as the reviewer's read, not a decision.
Probes were run from the open internet with no VPN/internal access, so "no response"
below means *not reachable from outside*, not necessarily dead.

Updated 2026-09-17: the apex mechanism is settled — the zone's nameservers move to
Cloudflare — and the [migration plan](#migration-plan) below was added.

Updated 2026-09-28: **step 1 is done.** The zone exists in Cloudflare, pending, as a
verified exact copy of Route53. Nothing user-visible has changed. Steps 2 and 3 below
are written as runbooks, each with its own rollback. The nameservers must change by
**2026-10-26**, or Cloudflare deletes the pending zone.
:::

## What M1 actually changes

Two records carry the entire cutover:

| Hostname | Type | Current target | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`bioconductor.org`]{#dns-bioconductor-org} (apex) | A, Route53 Alias | `d3hzwifbu1gvt4.cloudfront.net.` | The CloudFront distribution being retired |
| [`www.bioconductor.org`]{#dns-www-bioconductor-org} | A, Route53 Alias | `bioconductor.org.` | Aliases to the apex, not to CloudFront directly |

Both are live and serve the production site ("Bioconductor - Home") today. Everything
else in the zone is satellite: conference sites, mailing-list infrastructure, build
machines, DKIM keys. None of it needs to change for the site itself to move — it either
already points off AWS, or points at AWS/Jetstream2 resources this cutover doesn't touch.

### The apex is the hard part

Route53 "Alias" records — the mechanism used for the apex today — only resolve to AWS
resources (CloudFront, ELB, S3, another record in the same zone, etc.). They cannot
target an arbitrary external host like `bioc-dev.cancerdatasci.org`, and a plain CNAME
isn't legal at a zone apex per the DNS spec. `www.bioconductor.org` doesn't have this
problem — it's not the apex, so it can become a normal CNAME to the new edge once the
zone is ready. **Decision (2026-09-17): move the zone's nameservers to Cloudflare.**
Cloudflare flattens a CNAME at the apex, so the apex can target the Worker directly,
and AWS leaves the DNS path entirely. The domain *registration* stays at AWS; only the
nameservers change.

Rejected: a thin CloudFront distribution as a pass-through, origin set to
`bioc-dev.cancerdatasci.org`, with the Route53 Alias repointed at it. It moves no
records, but keeps AWS in the request path indefinitely and adds a cache-miss
origin-fetch charge (~$0.02/GB) on top of viewer egress.

## Migration plan {#migration-plan}

Two separately reversible steps. **Step one** moves the zone to Cloudflare as an exact
copy, apex still resolving to today's CloudFront distribution — users see nothing, and
anything that breaks is a mis-copied record. **Step two**, later, repoints the apex
and `www` at the new edge — flipped and rolled back by one proxy toggle per record.

The zone lives in the **current Cloudflare account** (the one that already holds the
`bioc-site` Worker, Workers Paid and R2 Paid). Moving to a dedicated Bioconductor
account is deferred; see [Cloudflare account migration](cloudflare-account-migration.qmd).

## Deadline: switch nameservers by 2026-10-26
Cloudflare deletes a Free-plan zone that stays **Pending** for 28 days. This one was
created 2026-09-28 15:22 UTC. If it lapses nothing breaks — Route53 is still
authoritative — but the zone must be re-added and re-imported (below), and Cloudflare
will likely assign different nameservers.
:::

How the copy was made, so it can be redone:

- `dns/route53-index.txt` — every record's name, type and TTL, read from the Route53
  console (152 records; Route53 allows no zone transfer and the available AWS role has
  no CloudShell).
- `dns/export-zone.sh` — asks Route53's own nameserver for every value in the index and
  writes `dns/bioconductor.org.zone`. `dns/bioconductor.org.cloudflare-import.zone` is
  the same minus the two records that were added by hand (below).
- Imported through the dashboard's zone-file upload. **That upload marks every A and
  CNAME record Proxied with TTL Auto** — all 110 were reset to DNS-only with their
  Route53 TTLs through the API. Any re-import must do the same.
- `dns/verify-zone.sh` — compares every record between two nameservers; exit status is
  the number of differences.

Deliberate differences from Route53:

| Record | Route53 | Cloudflare | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| apex `bioconductor.org` | Alias A → `d3hzwifbu1gvt4.cloudfront.net` | CNAME (flattened) → same, DNS only, TTL 300 | Aliases are Route53-only |
| `www` | Alias A → apex | CNAME → `bioconductor.org` | same |
| `testweb` | Alias → `d3h1507zzd6849.cloudfront.net` | **not copied** | That distribution no longer exists; Route53 already answers nothing |
| `bbr`, `*.bbr` | weighted: 200 → 149.165.153.78, 0 → 104.45.191.146 (AKS fallback) with health checks | single A → 149.165.153.78 | Failover needs Cloudflare Load Balancing; both are delete candidates |
| TXT on a literal `@.bioconductor.org` label | present | **not copied** | Cloudflare rejects the name; it's a data-entry error, the real SPF is at the apex |
| NS, SOA | AWS | Cloudflare's own | expected |

### 2. Change the nameservers

#### 2a. Lower the Route53 NS TTL — at least 2 days before 2b

After a nameserver change, a resolver keeps using the old nameservers until its cached
NS record expires. There are two copies of that record: the .org registry's (3600 s,
not ours to change) and the one the *old* provider serves itself, which some resolvers
prefer. So each direction's tail is set by the provider being left:

| Direction | TTLs that matter | Worst-case tail |
|---|---|---|
| Switch to Cloudflare (2b) | .org 1 h; **Route53 NS** — 172800 s today, 3600 s after this step | 2 days → 1 hour |
| Roll back to Route53 | .org 1 h; **Cloudflare NS**, 86400 s | 1 day, whatever we do here |

**This step shortens the switch, not a rollback.** Cloudflare's NS TTL is adjustable
only as part of Foundation DNS (Enterprise), so on this zone it is fixed at a day.
The step is still worth doing for two reasons:

- It shrinks the window in which Route53 and Cloudflare must both be kept correct.
- It makes a *second* attempt after a rollback clean. Resolvers that re-fetch Route53's
  NS during a rollback cache it for the full TTL, so without this step the retry starts
  a fresh 2-day tail.

A TTL is a ceiling, not a wait. Each resolver's clock started at its last fetch, many
follow the parent's 1 hour, and some cap long TTLs. So most traffic moves within about
an hour either way, and the worst-case figures describe the last stragglers.

This changes no answers, only how long they are cached. It is safe to do any time.

In the AWS console (account 555219204010, the NIH DNS role):

1. Open **Route 53 → Hosted zones**
   (<https://us-east-1.console.aws.amazon.com/route53/v2/hostedzones>).
2. Click **bioconductor.org** (hosted zone ID `Z2LMJH3A2CQNZZ`).
3. On the **Records** tab, tick the checkbox of the row with
   **Record name** `bioconductor.org` and **Type** `NS`. It is the third row. Tick
   only that one row.
4. Click **Edit record** in the details panel on the right.
5. Leave **Record name** empty and **Record type** `NS`. **Do not touch the Value box.**
   It must still list exactly these four lines:
   ```
   ns-1784.awsdns-31.co.uk.
   ns-1459.awsdns-54.org.
   ns-876.awsdns-45.net.
   ns-91.awsdns-11.com.
   ```
6. In **TTL (seconds)**, replace `172800` with `3600`.
7. Click **Save**. The banner reads that the record was updated; the change status
   goes from PENDING to INSYNC within about a minute.
8. Check from a terminal — the second column must read `3600`:
   ```sh
   dig +norec +noall +answer @ns-1784.awsdns-31.co.uk bioconductor.org NS
   ```
9. Note the time. Step 2b should start **48 hours later**, when the last
   172800-second cache entries have expired. If it slips, nothing breaks: the switch
   just has a longer tail, and it doesn't change how fast a rollback is.

Equivalent with the AWS CLI, for anyone with a profile in that account:

```sh
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z2LMJH3A2CQNZZ \
  --change-batch '{"Changes":[{"Action":"UPSERT","ResourceRecordSet":{
    "Name":"bioconductor.org.","Type":"NS","TTL":3600,"ResourceRecords":[
      {"Value":"ns-1784.awsdns-31.co.uk."},{"Value":"ns-1459.awsdns-54.org."},
      {"Value":"ns-876.awsdns-45.net."},{"Value":"ns-91.awsdns-11.com."}]}}]}'
```

**Undo:** the same edit with `172800`. Nothing else in the zone needs a TTL change:
apex and `www` are already 300 s in the Cloudflare copy.

From here until two weeks after 2b: **record freeze.** Any change to the zone is made in
both Route53 and Cloudflare, or not at all — the rollback depends on Route53 being
right.

#### 2b. Switch

1. Re-verify on the day. The zone must not have drifted since the copy:
   ```sh
   ./dns/verify-zone.sh | tail -1        # must print "== 0 differing record(s)"
   B=will.ns.cloudflare.com ./dns/verify-zone.sh | tail -1
   ```
   Also confirm the Route53 console still says **Records (152)**. The script only
   checks names in the index, so a record added in Route53 since 2026-09-28 shows up
   as a count mismatch, not a diff — add it to Cloudflare and the index first.
2. Copy the two nameservers from the Cloudflare dashboard (**bioconductor.org →
   Overview**). Copy them; do not type them.
3. AWS console → **Route 53 → Registered domains → bioconductor.org → Actions → Edit
   name servers**. Replace the four `awsdns` entries with `brynne.ns.cloudflare.com`
   and `will.ns.cloudflare.com` (only those two). **Save.** Do not transfer the
   registration, and do not turn on DNSSEC.
4. Watch the parent:
   ```sh
   dig +short NS bioconductor.org @$(dig +short NS org. | head -1)
   ```
   It shows the Cloudflare pair within minutes. Then click **Check nameservers now**
   on the Cloudflare Overview page. The zone turns **Active**, and Cloudflare sends an
   email, within minutes to a few hours.
5. Post-checks once Active:
   - `A=1.1.1.1 ./dns/verify-zone.sh` and `A=8.8.8.8 ./dns/verify-zone.sh` — the
     public view against Cloudflare, expect 0.
   - `curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/ | grep -i via` still shows CloudFront.
   - Send a message to and from a `@bioconductor.org` address (forwardemail), and
     check a Brevo send.
   - `ssh -T git@git.bioconductor.org` still reaches gitolite.
   - Spot-check a GitHub Pages site (`blog.`) and a Netlify one (`bioc2026.`).

**Rollback:** Registered domains → bioconductor.org → Actions → Edit name servers →
put back exactly:

```
ns-1784.awsdns-31.co.uk
ns-1459.awsdns-54.org
ns-876.awsdns-45.net
ns-91.awsdns-11.com
```

Most resolvers move back within the parent's 1 hour. Cloudflare's own NS records carry
86400 s (not adjustable on this plan), so a few resolvers keep asking Cloudflare for up
to a day. That is harmless **only if the Cloudflare zone keeps serving the same data**.
On rollback, leave the Cloudflare zone in place and unchanged for at least two days
before deleting or editing it.

Only roll back the nameservers when Cloudflare's DNS *service* is the problem. A wrong
or missing record is faster to fix in Cloudflare itself (records carry 300 s TTLs),
and every resolver sees the fix, including the ones a rollback would leave behind.

**Afterwards:** leave the Route53 hosted zone untouched for at least two weeks (it's
the rollback target), then lift the freeze. Enable DNSSEC in Cloudflare only after
that, as its own change.

### 3. Flip the site (M1 proper)

**Mechanism: a Workers route plus the proxy toggle**, not a Workers Custom Domain.

- A route (`bioconductor.org/*` → `bioc-site`) only intercepts traffic on *proxied*
  records. It can be deployed days ahead and sits inert while apex and `www` are DNS
  only.
- The flip is switching those two records to **Proxied**. The rollback is switching them
  back to **DNS only**. At that point traffic goes straight to CloudFront again,
  because the CNAME to the CloudFront distribution never changed. That's two clicks,
  with no deploy and no record deletion.
- A Custom Domain needs the existing record deleted, then recreates and owns it
  itself. The rollback target would be gone and would have to be retyped under
  pressure.
- The routes go in `worker/wrangler.jsonc` in bioc-cloudflare, not the dashboard.
  `wrangler deploy` replaces a Worker's routes with the config's, so a dashboard-only
  route disappears on the next deploy.

Before the flip:

1. **Edge certificate.** After the zone goes Active: **SSL/TLS → Edge Certificates**
   must show the Universal certificate (`bioconductor.org`, `*.bioconductor.org`) as
   **Active**. Proxying before it is Active serves TLS errors. Set **SSL/TLS mode** to
   **Full (strict)**; CloudFront holds a valid certificate for the names, so any
   request the Worker passes to origin still verifies.
2. **Logging** ([ADR 0003](adr/0003-request-logging-after-the-cloudflare-cutover.md)):
   the Worker's Logpush job is delivering, and a record-count alert exists. Once
   traffic moves, CloudFront logs stop accruing.
3. **Plain HTTP.** Decide whether to turn **Always Use HTTPS** on (it matches
   production's 301). It only affects proxied names.
4. **Rehearse on a spare name.** Add `next.bioconductor.org` CNAME → `bioconductor.org`,
   Proxied, plus a route `next.bioconductor.org/*`. Run `cutover-diff.sh`
   (bioc-cloudflare) against it. This catches any place the Worker assumes the dev
   hostname.
5. **Deploy the routes** (inert until proxied). In `worker/wrangler.jsonc`:
   ```jsonc
   "routes": [
     { "pattern": "bioc-dev.cancerdatasci.org", "custom_domain": true },
     { "pattern": "bioconductor.org/*",     "zone_name": "bioconductor.org" },
     { "pattern": "www.bioconductor.org/*", "zone_name": "bioconductor.org" }
   ]
   ```
   Confirm under **Workers Routes** in the zone that both appear.

Flip: **DNS → Records**. On the `bioconductor.org` CNAME, click **Edit**, switch
**Proxy status** on, and **Save**. Repeat for `www`.

Verify:
- `curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/` and `https://www.bioconductor.org/` show
  `server: cloudflare` and no `via: … cloudfront`.
- Run `cutover-diff.sh` against production.
- Watch Workers → bioc-site → Metrics for errors, and the Logpush destination for
  records.

**Rollback:** the same two records, **Proxy status** off, then Save. Resolvers holding
Cloudflare's addresses expire within 300 s. Leave the routes deployed; they are inert
again. Keep CloudFront and `master` running until M2 retires them.

### Found along the way — fix separately, not during the move

- The spreadsheet lists a TXT record on a literal `@.bioconductor.org` label carrying
  `v=spf1 include:spf.forwardemail.net -all`. It is a data-entry mistake for the apex.
  Route53 serves it at that literal name, and Cloudflare refuses the name.
  **The apex has no SPF record at all** (checked 2026-09-28). Its TXT records are only
  `acevhogcbpv6dssaq15fbe1ek8`, a Brevo code and a forwardemail verification, and the
  `include:_spf.mlsend.com` SPF seen in the 2026-09 review is gone. With `_dmarc` at
  `p=reject`, mail from the domain now depends on DKIM alignment alone. Add a real
  apex SPF (forwardemail + Brevo + SES) as its own change, in both zones during the
  freeze.
- The apex TXT value `acevhogcbpv6dssaq15fbe1ek8` has no recorded owner.
- `testweb` is an Alias to a CloudFront distribution that no longer exists — delete it
  from Route53.
- `bbr`/`*.bbr` still carry a Route53 health-checked failover to an AKS address.
  Delete them, along with the health checks (which bill monthly).
- Since the 2026-09 review, several delete candidates are already gone (`tokay*`,
  `merida*`, `malbec*`, `machv2`, `celaya2`, `monitor`, `docbuilder`, `kjohnson1`,
  `meet`). New since then: `autoconfig`/`autodiscover` (forwardemail), `status`,
  `testgalaxy`, `eurobioc2027`, the Brevo DKIM selectors. Many A-record targets also
  moved (e.g. `workshop` is now 149.165.152.155). The per-host detail below predates
  this and is not re-probed.

## Core infrastructure, staying put (27)

Marked "keep" in the source review, not touched by the M1 apex/www flip. Visited each directly (`curl -sI https://<host>/`) rather than assuming from the hostname.

### `master.bioconductor.org` {#dns-master-bioconductor-org}

A → `52.71.54.154`. Live — full production `bioconductor.org` mirror. This is the legacy master webserver being retired by the M1/M2 migration.

### `staging.bioconductor.org` {#dns-staging-bioconductor-org}

A → `52.4.245.79`. No public HTTPS response. Confirmed elsewhere in this repo (see the [decommission plan](decommission-plan.qmd)) that no web server listens here — this is the legacy build host, not a public site.

### `git.bioconductor.org` {#dns-git-bioconductor-org}

A → `34.192.48.227`. Confirmed live: gitolite3 v3.6.6 serving the package git repos directly (`admin/…`, `packages/ABAData`, …) — this *is* the canonical package source, not a redirect target.

### `chat.bioconductor.org` {#dns-chat-bioconductor-org}

A → `34.192.48.227`. Same redirect target as `zulip.bioconductor.org` — an alias into the same Zulip Cloud instance.

### `zulip.bioconductor.org` {#dns-zulip-bioconductor-org}

A → `34.192.48.227`. Redirects to the team's hosted Zulip Cloud instance (`community-bioc.zulipchat.com`) — the real chat entry point.

### `www.zulip.bioconductor.org` {#dns-www-zulip-bioconductor-org}

A → `34.192.48.227`. No public response. Shares its target IP with `zulip`/`chat`/`git`/`packages` — routing for `www.`-prefixed vhosts on that box looks inconsistent.

### `www.chat.bioconductor.org` {#dns-www-chat-bioconductor-org}

A → `34.192.48.227`. No public response, same shared-IP pattern as `www.zulip`.

### `packages.bioconductor.org` {#dns-packages-bioconductor-org}

A → `34.192.48.227`. Redirects to the Open Storage Network archive bucket — a convenience alias so people don't need the full OSN URL to browse package archives.

### `support.bioconductor.org` {#dns-support-bioconductor-org}

A → `54.164.10.157`. Live — the Bioconductor Support Forum (Django app, Biostars-derived).

### `issues.bioconductor.org` {#dns-issues-bioconductor-org}

A → `52.4.116.154`. Responds but the body is literally "Nothing to see here" — currently a stub. Worth checking whether the real issue tracker moved elsewhere, or this is mid-decommission.

### `code.bioconductor.org` {#dns-code-bioconductor-org}

A → `194.94.45.72`. No public HTTPS response — purpose unconfirmed from outside; worth a direct look.

## Already off AWS — no action (27, one table)

Event-site CNAMEs (`bioc20{18..26}`, `biocasia20{20..26}`, `eurobioc20{19..26}`,
`gbcc2025`) plus `dev.status`, and `fe-bounces` — all confirmed live, all pointing at
GitHub Pages, Netlify, or forwardemail.net. None resolve through CloudFront, master, or
staging — the cutover is invisible to them.

## Delete candidates (25) — confirmed unreachable

Every host in this list returned no public HTTPS response in the probe, consistent with
being retired already: `tokay1/2`, `merida1/2`, `malbec1/2`, `machv2`, `celaya2`,
`monitor`, `docbuilder`, `kjohnson1`, `k8slaunch`, `js2launch`, `bbr` (×2),
`yescure(cluster)`, `prodaks` — plus seven tagged "delete end of 2026"
(`workshopk8s`, `workshopcluster`, `prodk8s`, `hsdsdev`, `cloudman.kubeinstall`,
`ci-mirror`, `biocworkshop`), presumably tied to a class or grant ending. The probe is
supporting evidence for the delete call, not proof — "no public HTTPS" doesn't rule out
an internal-only service still in use.

## Mail/cert plumbing and wildcards, undecided (24)

Not individually probed — none of these are meant to serve HTTP content. ACM
certificate-validation CNAMEs (`_....acm-validations.aws.`) and DKIM selector CNAMEs
need re-verification against whatever currently sends mail as `bioconductor.org`, not
assumption of obsolescence. The wildcard records (`*.workshop`, `*.auth`, `*.bbr`, …)
mirror a decision already made on their base hostname above but weren't themselves
tagged — worth confirming they're meant to inherit it rather than being reviewed
independently.

## Open questions for the core team

- ~~Apex mechanism~~ — settled 2026-09-17: nameserver migration to Cloudflare, see the
  [migration plan](#migration-plan).
- Dedicated Bioconductor Cloudflare account: deferred until after the cutover; see
  [Cloudflare account migration](cloudflare-account-migration.qmd). Still needs super
  administrators and a billing owner named.
- R2 object count for `bioc-site` and `bioc-prop` — sizes the account-move copy (time
  and write-operation cost).
- Plain-HTTP behaviour on the new edge: redirect to HTTPS like production, or serve 200?
- Which SPF record is intended at the apex, and who owns the unlisted apex TXT value?
- `new.bioconductor.org` mirrors `master.bioconductor.org` exactly (same IP, same
  content) — leftover alias or intentional?
- `slack.bioconductor.org` serves a generic template unrelated to its name — check what
  this vhost is actually for.
- `issues.bioconductor.org` responds with a bare "Nothing to see here" — confirm whether
  the real tracker moved.
- Confirm the 18 undecided hosts above, especially the stale-looking test hosts
  (`testweb`, `testinggit`, `gitdevtest`, `gitdevtest2`, `support.test`) and the
  second CloudFront distribution behind `testweb` (`d3h1507zzd6849.cloudfront.net`,
  distinct from production — does it need retiring too?).
